newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends a tad higher in US, eyes payrolls, Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends a tad higher in US, eyes payrolls, Rubin.

text.p: The dollar edged modestly higher on Thursday in a subdued, rangebound U.S. session as traders squared positions ahead of key U.S. payrolls data.

After opening at lower levels on the heels of strong German industrial data and a yen-supportive report from the International Monetary Fund, the greenback settled down to drift in a tight range between 122.50 and 122.85 yen and 1.6650 and 1.6710 marks.
"There are very few position holders in this market," said Bob Savage, chief dealer at Lehman Brothers.
"How can you be aggressive ahead of an employment report which many will use as a barometer of whether the Fed is on top of the growth and inflation story," he added.
The dollar ended the day at 122.59/64 yen, slightly higher than its opening rate of 122.50/60, but off Wednesday's close of 123.25/35.
Against the mark, the dollar settled at 1.6700/05, also a tad higher than its opening rate of 1.6690/00, but off Wednesday's 1.6770/80 close.

With U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin scheduled to arrive in Japan on Friday for meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, the hot issue of U.S./Japan trade also weighed on the market.
U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky reiterated on Thursday that the U.S. does not expect to see an increase in the trade gap between the two countries.
Meanwhile, Japanese Ministry of Finance officials tried to nip any incipient trade tensions in the bud, saying they did not expect the Japanese trade surplus to expand drastically.

Despite nervousness about Rubin's trip, players resisted pushing dollar/yen lower during U.S. trade on Thursday, cheered in part by overnight statements from Japan's Postal Life Insurance Bureau -- Kampo.
Kampo told Reuters that it might boost its foreign bond purchases and that it expected dollar/yen to stay above the 120 level in the near-term.
"There's a little nervousness about Rubin but the market is talking about the Kampo story," said Lehman's Savage.
The dollar's upside against the mark was kept in check by strong German industrial output figures for February, dealers said.
German industrial production, driven by manufacturing strength and a seasonal rebound in construction, rose 1.9 percent in February over January and by 7.1 percent over February of 1996.
An IMF paper, scheduled to be presented at a meeting of Asia-Pacific finance officials over the weekend, helped cap dollar/yen, traders said.
The report said that the yen's depreciation since reaching post-World War II highs in early 1995 had corrected misalignments, but also noted that some of the yen's fall could be reversed.
"I think we're just really smack back in neutral territory in dollar/yen," said Bob Near, vice president on the corporate foreign exchange desk at Bank of New York.
Overall, dealers stressed that trading had turned extremely subdued ahead of Friday's jobs report.
Wall Street economists are expecting a rise of 196,000 in March payrolls after February's heady gain of 339,000.
"What we are looking for at this point is some sense as to whether interest rates are going up or not," said Hillel Waxman, chief foreign exchange dealer at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
"Until that number comes out and we see the reaction of the bond and stock market, the dollar won't be able to do much."
In other trade on Thursday, the dollar pushed up to its highest level in two years against the Canadian dollar, ending at C$1.3925/30, against C$1.3851/56 at the open.
The dollar settled at 1.4340/50 Swiss francs, slightly up from 1.4330/40, while the British pound rose to $1.6444/54 from $1.6400/10.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7780/85 down from $0.7802/07.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
